hook: the short surahs; the mountain ahead

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prophet, peace be upon him, the orphan Mecca called al-Amin, the trustworthy. Did you keep that small promise? Day twenty-one.

Three weeks. Look at what's on your strand. Salaam. Bismillah. Alhamdulillah. Inshallah. The five pillars. Then al-Fatiha, verse by verse: Rabb, rahma, the Day, tawhid, the straight path, amin. Wudu, salat, the adhan. Jumu'ah. Dhikr. Ramadan and zakat. The Prophet, al-Amin. Twenty words, the everyday vocabulary of a Muslim life. That's the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing: the stories of the prophets, one after another. So today, at the top of the foothills, we look up at the mountain itself. The Qur'an. And we find the place where almost every Muslim starts to climb it. Oddly enough, it's at the very end.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `THE FOOTHILLS, DONE.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has a hundred and fourteen surahs, roughly longest first, shortest last. To make it possible to read the whole thing in a month, especially in Ramadan, it's divided into thirty equal parts. Each part is a juz'. The last one is called juz' 'amma, after its very first word. Surah seventy-eight opens, in Pickthall's words: “Whereof do they question one another?” In Arabic, 'amma yatasa'alun. So 'amma, whereof, gives the whole part its name. Juz' 'amma holds thirty-seven surahs, from seventy-eight to the end. Most are short, some only three or four lines. Many scholars place most of them among the earliest revelations in Mecca: vivid, rhythmic, full of oaths by the dawn, the night, the fig, the declining day. And this is where children begin. Not at page one, at the back. A child learns al-Fatiha, then an-Nas, the last surah, and al-Falaq, and al-Ikhlas, which you met on day ten. Then al-Kawthar, the shortest in the whole Qur'an, three verses. Then al-'Asr, and so on, backward, surah by surah. These are the ones a Muslim recites in the daily prayers, again and again, for a lifetime. Grandparents and five-year-olds know the same ones by heart. For some, the climb goes on for years, all the way up, until the whole Qur'an is held in memory; someone who does that is called a hafiz, a keeper. But almost everyone starts here, at the small end of the mountain.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS, FOR A MONTH.` · `'AMMA — WHEREOF DO THEY QUESTION?` · `THE EARLIEST, SHORTEST SURAHS.` · `CHILDREN START AT THE BACK.` · then, large: `THE SMALL END OF THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past, the greeting, the washing, the call, the fast, the one. Don't try to remember all of them. Just notice which one has stuck. Which one came back to you on an ordinary day, in the kitchen or the car, without being asked? Hold that one word. It's yours now. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. The bell holds the time.
Juz' 'amma. The thirtieth part of the Qur'an, the short surahs, where nearly everyone begins. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
Your line: the ones every Muslim child knows. Today, look up surah one hundred and three, al-'Asr, three lines, and read it once. Tomorrow, the stories begin. Day twenty-one.

what it means: juz' 'amma — the thirtieth of thirty parts, surahs 78 to 114, the short surahs every Muslim child knows and every prayer uses.

what a scholar hears: the parts are a reading division, not the revelation's own; the surahs run roughly longest to shortest; and many of the last part's surahs are placed among the earliest Meccan revelations.
